summary: Defines CMC, a protocol for requesting and managing public key certificates using messages wrapped in the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS). It lets clients and certificate authorities exchange requests, responses and related management messages. It is on the standards track and was replaced by RFC 5272.

eli5.summary: Imagine a club that hands out membership cards. This is the standard form and envelope you use to ask for a card, and the way the club sends it back safely.

questions: how to request a certificate using cms
subtitle: A protocol for requesting and managing public key certificates using standard cryptographic messages.

tldr.problem: Certificate authorities need a standard way for clients to request certificates, and clients need a way to ask for multiple certificates in one request, handle certificate renewal, work with intermediate registration authorities, and prove they own the private key.
tldr.mechanism: CMC (Certificate Management Messages over CMS) wraps certificate requests in the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS), allowing clients to send PKCS#10 or CRMF requests bundled with additional control attributes like proof of key possession, authentication, and transaction tracking. Servers respond with signed certificate bundles.
tldr.outcome: Clients and CAs can exchange certificate requests and responses in a standard, flexible way that supports authentication, encryption, multiple keys, and deferred issuance. This RFC was superseded by RFC 5272.

today: RFC 2797 is now Historic, superseded by RFC 5272 (published 2008). The newer RFC refines the protocol with additional clarifications and support for updated cryptographic standards. Though obsolete as a standards-track specification, CMC concepts remain widely used in PKI systems.

sections.title: Certificate Management Over CMS
sections.content:
Public Key Infrastructure (PKI) requires a standard way for clients to request digital certificates from certificate authorities (CAs). Early solutions used separate request and response formats, making it hard to request multiple certificates, add extra information, or handle complex scenarios.

CMC addresses these needs by using the Cryptographic Message Syntax (CMS) as a transport wrapper. CMS is a standard for signed and encrypted messages that is already used for email security and other purposes. By wrapping certificate requests in CMS, CMC provides authentication, encryption, and flexibility while staying compatible with existing PKI practices.
sections.eli5: Instead of inventing a new way to ask for certificates, use the same envelope format (CMS) that people already use for secure email. Put your request inside, sign it so the CA knows it is you, and the CA sends back your certificates in the same kind of envelope.

sections.title: Protocol Modes and Message Flow
sections.content:
CMC defines two simple request and response modes. The Simple Enrollment Request is just a PKCS#10 or CRMF certificate request, optionally signed with the private key being certified (to prove key possession). The Simple Enrollment Response is a CMS signedData object containing the issued certificates and any intermediate CA certificates, with no additional data.

The Full Enrollment Request wraps the certificate request(s) and additional control attributes in a PKIData object, all signed in a CMS signedData wrapper. This allows a single request to include multiple keys, authentication credentials, and ancillary data. The Full Enrollment Response is a ResponseBody object signed in CMS, allowing the server to return status information, deferred responses, or error details.

Most transactions use simple mode, but advanced scenarios like batch enrollment, key renewal, or interactions with registration authorities (RAs) use the full mode.
sections.eli5: Simple request: "Here is my public key, signed with my private key (so you know I have it). Please issue a certificate." Simple response: "Here are your certificates." Full request: "Here is my key, plus proof I am real, plus a bunch of other keys I want, all in one package." Full response: "Your certificates are ready, or they are pending, with extra details."

sections.title: Request Structure and Certificate Requests
sections.content:
A PKIData object contains four sequences: control attributes, certificate requests, CMS objects, and other messages. Control attributes are OID-value pairs that specify operations like transaction management, proof of key possession, and identity proof. Certificate requests can be PKCS#10 (a simple format from RSA Labs) or CRMF (a more complex format that supports attributes and recovery information).

Each element in a PKIData has a Body Part Identifier, a unique number used to reference it in responses and control attributes. The ID 0 is reserved to mean the PKIData object itself.

For clients using Diffie-Hellman keys (which cannot directly sign), CMC provides special mechanisms: the "no-signature" method (just a hash), or the Diffie-Hellman proof-of-possession signature methods defined in a separate specification.
sections.eli5: Inside the request envelope: a list of instructions ("do this"), a list of "I want a certificate for this key," and any extra data. Each piece gets a number so the response can say "your request #3 was approved" or "your request #5 failed."

sections.title: Response Messages and Status Reporting
sections.content:
A ResponseBody object mirrors PKIData with control attributes, CMS objects, and other messages, but no certificate requests. The server returns control attributes to report status, indicate pending or deferred responses, or describe errors. Each response is tied to a body part ID from the request, allowing precise error reporting.

Servers include all issued certificates in the CMS signedData object's certificate bag. Intermediate CA certificates and CRLs (Certificate Revocation Lists) should be included to form a complete chain. Servers SHOULD include all intermediate certificates needed to validate back to a trusted root, not just the newly issued certificate.

If a request cannot be fulfilled immediately, the server returns a pending or deferred status, allowing the client to poll for completion later. This supports workflows where certificate issuance requires manual review or external validation.
sections.eli5: The response has similar pieces: a status report ("approved", "pending", or "error"), the certificates (with their chain of trust), and optional extra data. Each response points back to the request it answers, so if you asked for three certificates, you know which ones succeeded and which ones failed.

sections.title: Advanced Features and Registration Authorities
sections.content:
CMC supports several advanced features. Proof of Possession (POP) proves the client owns the private key corresponding to the public key being certified. Methods include signing the request with the private key, or (for Diffie-Hellman) using a special signature algorithm.

CMC allows arbitrary chains of Local Registration Authorities (LRAs). An LRA receives a request from an end-entity, adds its own control attributes (such as identity verification data), and forwards the expanded request to the next LRA or the CA. Each layer can add requirements or vouching.

Transaction IDs and nonces prevent replay attacks and allow clients to match responses to requests. Encrypted envelopes allow sensitive data (like private key material for key archival) to be included in requests and responses.

CMC also supports certificate renewal and re-keying: the client signs the new request with an existing certificate, proving their identity without needing separate identity proof.
sections.eli5: You can prove you have the private key. You can work through middlemen (RAs) who add their own stamps of approval. You can use a number to match the response to your request. You can send private data encrypted. You can renew a certificate by signing the new request with your old certificate.
